target: Il a dit qu'il viendrait demain.
english: He said he would come tomorrow.
tip: For a 'would' in reported speech, French uses the conditional: 'il viendrait' = he would come. It's the future seen from a past moment.

target: Elle est montée au troisième étage.
english: She went up to the third floor.
tip: With être the participle agrees in writing only: 'est montée' adds an -e for she, but it sounds exactly like 'monté'.

target: Il ressemblait beaucoup à son père.
english: He looked a lot like his father.
tip: Ressembler always takes à – you resemble to someone: 'ressemblait à son père'. There's no direct object the way English 'looks like him' has.

target: Nous vendions des légumes au marché.
english: We used to sell vegetables at the market.
tip: The imparfait 'vendions' covers English 'used to sell' – a repeated past habit. No extra words needed; the tense alone carries the used-to.

target: J'ai marché le long de la rivière.
english: I walked along the river.
tip: 'Le long de' means along – literally 'the length of': 'le long de la rivière'. It's a fixed three-word unit, always ending in de.

target: Elle a ouvert la lettre avec impatience.
english: She opened the letter impatiently.
tip: French often turns a noun into an adverb with avec: 'avec impatience' = impatiently. Common even where a -ment adverb like impatiemment exists.

target: Nous avons fini le projet vendredi dernier.
english: We finished the project last Friday.
tip: 'Vendredi dernier' (last Friday) – 'dernier' goes after days/months: lundi dernier, le mois dernier.

target: Il a été malade pendant une semaine.
english: He was sick for a week.
tip: Être builds its own past with avoir, not itself: 'il a été malade' = he was sick. Never 'il est été'.

target: Elle a oublié son parapluie au bureau.
english: She forgot her umbrella at the office.
tip: Son agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: 'son parapluie' is her umbrella here as easily as his. The gender follows parapluie.

target: Il a été professeur pendant vingt ans.
english: He was a teacher for twenty years.
tip: Drop the article before a job: 'il a été professeur' = he was a teacher, with no 'un'. The profession behaves like an adjective after être.

target: Tu as fait attention en traversant la rue ?
english: Did you pay attention while crossing the street?
tip: French 'makes' attention rather than paying it: 'faire attention' = to pay attention or to be careful.

target: Il y avait toujours du monde dans ce restaurant.
english: There were always people in this restaurant.
tip: 'Il y avait' is simply the past of 'il y a' (there is): 'il y avait du monde' = there were people. One fixed phrase, not a verb to conjugate.

target: Il faisait beau quand nous avons quitté la maison.
english: The weather was nice when we left the house.
tip: 'Il faisait beau' (weather = background) + 'nous avons quitté' (completed departure). Classic contrast.

target: Nous sommes passés par le centre-ville.
english: We went through the city center.
tip: Passer flips helpers by meaning: être for moving through ('nous sommes passés par...'), but avoir for spending time – j'ai passé une semaine.

target: Il pleuvait sans arrêt pendant nos vacances.
english: It was raining non-stop during our vacation.
tip: 'Sans arrêt' (non-stop) reinforces the ongoing, continuous nature – classic imparfait context.

target: Elle est sortie avec ses collègues vendredi.
english: She went out with her colleagues on Friday.
tip: Sortir uses être: elle est sortie. Agreement with feminine subject.

target: Ils ont joué au football dans le parc.
english: They played football in the park.
tip: 'Jouer' forms passé composé with 'avoir': ils ont joué. Only movement/state-change verbs use 'être'.

target: Ils sont morts dans un accident de voiture.
english: They died in a car accident.
tip: 'Ils sont morts' looks like 'they are dead' but it's the past of mourir: 'they died'. Mourir takes être.

target: Elle travaillait dans une librairie à cette époque.
english: She worked in a bookstore at that time.
tip: 'À cette époque' (back then) is a cue for the imparfait: 'travaillait' paints how life was, not a single finished event.

target: Il neigeait dehors et nous restions au chaud.
english: It was snowing outside and we stayed warm.
tip: Weather descriptions in the past use imparfait: il neigeait, il pleuvait, il faisait froid.

target: Ils devaient prendre le train de sept heures.
english: They had to take the seven o'clock train.
tip: 'Ils devaient' = they were supposed to, leaving it open whether they did. 'Ils ont dû' would mean they had to and actually did.

target: Nous sommes allés à la plage le week-end dernier.
english: We went to the beach last weekend.
tip: Verbs of movement like aller take être, not avoir: 'nous sommes allés' = we went. Most other verbs use avoir.

target: Il pleuvait depuis deux heures quand le soleil est apparu.
english: It had been raining for two hours when the sun appeared.
tip: English 'had been raining' is just imparfait + depuis in French: 'il pleuvait depuis deux heures' = it had been raining for two hours.

target: Il faisait beau ce jour-là.
english: The weather was nice that day.
tip: 'Il faisait beau' – weather in the past uses imparfait because it describes a backdrop/state.

target: Je croyais qu'il était médecin.
english: I thought he was a doctor.
tip: French drops 'a' before a job: 'il était médecin', not un médecin. Same for any profession after être – elle est avocate, il est prof.

target: Nous avons eu beaucoup de chance.
english: We were very lucky.
tip: Luck is something you HAVE in French, not something you are: 'avons eu beaucoup de chance' = had a lot of luck, so 'we were very lucky'.

target: Tu as fait la vaisselle ?
english: Did you do the dishes?
tip: 'La vaisselle' is singular – all the dishes as one heap. You don't wash them, you 'faire la vaisselle', literally do the dishware.

target: Il a pris une décision importante.
english: He made an important decision.
tip: You don't 'make' a decision in French, you take one: 'a pris une décision'. It's prendre, not faire, that goes with décision.

target: J'ai bu un café bien serre.
english: I drank a strong coffee.
tip: A strong espresso is 'serré' – literally tight or squeezed. 'Un café bien serré' packs the same coffee into less water.

target: Ils ont dit qu'ils viendraient samedi.
english: They said they would come on Saturday.
tip: Reporting a future from the past? French uses the conditional: 'ils viendraient' = they would come. Said back then, it still points forward.
